claims.text: Reactive consolidation can overcome the positive heat of mixing between refractory high-entropy alloy components and Cu.
The proposed process enables large-scale synthesis of a refractory-HEA/Cu composite.
The resulting refractory-HEA/Cu composite will be well bonded and microstructurally stable under nuclear-reactor conditions.
The precursor consists of refractory HEA powders and Cu particles.
The refractory-HEA/Cu precursor has limited interfacial reactivity because of thermodynamic repulsion.
The reactive consolidation route consists of high-energy ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering.
A machine-learning model integrating thermodynamic and kinetic simulations can optimize the temperature ramp, peak temperature, pressure, and dwell time.
High pressure and rapid heating kinetically activate localized reactions at refractory-HEA/Cu interfaces.
The processing conditions simulate both the high-temperature and irradiation environments of next-generation nuclear reactors.
Reactive consolidation forms intermediate or metastable phases at the refractory-HEA/Cu interface.
A refined interfacial reaction zone enhances bonding between the refractory matrix and Cu.
Optimized high-energy processing kinetically overcomes thermodynamic repulsion and promotes a controlled interfacial reaction.
The controlled interfacial reaction yields a coherent and stable composite microstructure.
Reactive consolidation will significantly improve interfacial bonding relative to conventional processing.
Reactive consolidation will refine the composite microstructure relative to conventional processing.
Reactive consolidation will enhance mechanical integrity relative to conventional processing.
Reactive consolidation will provide superior thermal stability relative to conventional processing.
Conventional solid-state processing fails to induce sufficient refractory-HEA/Cu interfacial reaction and therefore produces poorly bonded, unstable microstructures.

Successful scale-up requires uniform maintenance of optimized processing parameters, and deviations in energy input or temperature control may reduce interfacial reaction quality and microstructural stability.
The optimal temperature, pressure, and dwell-time thresholds remain uncertain and require experimental validation.
